newsitem.title: UK: UK life insurers slow to use technology - manager.
newsitem.headline: UK life insurers slow to use technology - manager.

text.p: UK life insurers are failing to take full advantage of inter-active technology, limiting themselves largely to using it as a one-way advertising medium, an industry expert said on Thursday.

"Most insurers have web-sites but are they really interested in exploiting the technology or is it just a 'me too' fad? I think it's often the latter," Ingrid Brandon, head of M&G Re's electronic distribution team, said in an address to the Insurance Institute of London.
Judges in a recent competition for the best insurance Internet sites found the overall design poor, noted Brandon, who sees many life insurers through her work for Swiss Re -owned life reinsurer M&G.
However, technology was only a facilitator of business success, Brandon said. A greater challenge facing the life insurance industry was the need to change the focus of its products.
Most product design dates from the 1970s and is company and shareholder value based rather than customer and service focused, with policies being complex and sending negative messages to customers.
"The industry needs to undergo a radical re-appraisal if it is to compete with some of the new players...Traditional life companies are very vulnerable to attack," Brandon said.
Mis-selling of both pensions and mortgages had also tarnished the industry's image in the eyes of many consumers, she added.
By contrast, direct car and home insurers such as Direct Line and Churchill had demonstrated how a simplified, customer-based approach could break the stranglehold of traditional insurers.

Against this background new entrants were moving into the life insurance market, often using brand names -- such as Marks & Spencer and Virgin -- which were successful and trusted in other retail markets.
Technology was only part of the answer to this threat, Brandon said, adding that it was more important to provide better service and change many of the industry's processes.
"People want service not technology...Having all the technology in the world isn't going to work for you; people hold the key to success."
Business retention and service levels should be used by companies as a measure of success rather than new business volumes, she added.
The cost of technology should not be seen as a barrier to its use, Brandon said.
However, the cost factor was contributing to the ongoing consolidation within the life industry and more alliances and partnerships could be expected to share the cost of new systems.
Apart from direct telephone selling, armchair multimedia such as interactive television and home personal computer-based internet services offered considerable scope for low cost sales.
"The convergence of all technologies will shape the future of distribution," Brandon said, urging companies to think in terms of combinations of technologies.
